name: Model State Vital Statistics Act (CDC/NCHS)
note: The CDC/NCHS Model State Vital Statistics Act is the template most State death-registration laws follow. Under it, the funeral director files the death certificate with the State vital records office within 5 days of death and before final disposition. The attending physician certifies the cause within 48 hours, medicolegal deaths go to the medical examiner, and an authorization for final disposition depends on filing. Copies are limited to people with a direct and tangible interest. CDC's own site was unreachable, so this file is unverified throughout.

steps.title: Informant supplies personal data to the funeral director
steps.who: The next of kin or other informant.
steps.summary: The funeral director gets the personal data from the next of kin or best qualified person available.

steps.title: Physician completes the medical certification within 48 hours
steps.who: The physician in charge of the patient's care for the illness or condition that resulted in death.
steps.trigger: Delivery of the certificate by the funeral director.
steps.summary: The attending physician completes, signs and returns the medical certification within 48 hours after death, except where the death must be referred to the medical examiner.

steps.title: Medicolegal deaths go to the medical examiner or coroner
steps.who: The funeral director, physician or other person aware of the death.
steps.trigger: A death without medical attendance or under circumstances requiring medicolegal investigation.
steps.summary: Deaths that occur without medical attendance or are reportable under the State's medicolegal law are referred to the medical examiner or coroner, who completes the medical certification.

steps.title: Funeral director files the death certificate within 5 days and before final disposition
steps.who: The funeral director or person acting as such who first assumes custody of the body.

deadline.text: within 5 days after death and prior to final disposition

steps.summary: A death certificate for each death in the State is filed with the State office of vital statistics (or as the State Registrar directs) within 5 days after death or the finding of the body, and before final disposition.

steps.title: Authorization for final disposition
steps.who: The local registrar or other official designated by the State Registrar.
steps.trigger: Filing of the death certificate (or its medical certification).
steps.summary: The funeral director must obtain an authorization for final disposition before burial, cremation or removal from the State, which ties disposition to registration.

steps.title: Certified copies only to applicants with a direct and tangible interest
steps.summary: Vital records are not public. Certified copies are issued only to applicants with a direct and tangible interest (registrant's family, legal representatives) or for official purposes, and records become open after a set number of years.

registrationDeadlineDays.note: Within 5 days after death and before final disposition (1992 revision, unverified).

informantDuty.note: The funeral director files; the next of kin supplies personal data.

gaps: www.cdc.gov and stacks.cdc.gov were refused at the egress proxy (CONNECT 403; WebFetch reported the host as outside the allowed domains), so no Model Act text could be read. Every step and feature is unverified, and the citations deliberately carry no section numbers.

The 2011 revision named in the research request was not found on any CDC host. Search results indicate NAPHSIS approved it in 2011 but CDC never published it, and NAPHSIS released a draft in 2013 that is now members-only. The citations therefore point to the CDC-published 1992 revision (mvsact92b.pdf). Whether the 2011 draft changes the 5-day/48-hour deadlines (or adds a 3-day funeral-director step) is unknown.

The Model Act's provisions on electronic filing, on the State Registrar's exchanges with SSA/NCHS, and on matching deaths to birth records were not checked, so electronicRegistration and governmentPropagation are left out.
The NCHS Funeral Director's Handbook (stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/80634) and the Physicians' Handbook on death certification would corroborate the model deadlines, but both are on blocked CDC hosts.
